title: Speed-to-scale claim experiments and field scripts
content:
Objective:

This is a working brief for a small set of claim experiments and field scripts focused on demonstrating Redwood Inference as the practical "speed-to-scale" partner: faster end-to-end user latency and measurably lower per-active-user inference cost under realistic workloads. The goal is to produce a tightly scoped set of sales-ready proof points plus a repeatable experiment plan so AE/SE teams can run lightweight on-site demos or remote recordings.

Audience:
- AEs/SEs running technical buys for mid-market SaaS and AI-native startups.
- Platform/Infra buyers evaluating dedicated capacity or private deployments.
- Customer engineering teams doing bake-offs against self-hosted runtimes.

Primary claims to validate (working wording):
1) "Perceived latency: Redwood reduces end-to-end 95th pct user-perceived latency by 30–60% vs typical managed endpoints at similar throughput."
2) "Unit cost: For production conversational workloads, Redwood's batching + cache + routing stack reduces cost-per-active-user by 20–50% compared to default single-instance hosted endpoints, and by 10–30% vs naïve self-hosted GPU deployments when including ops amortization."
3) "Sensible degradation: During load spikes, Redwood’s automatic fallback routing keeps p99 latency within X2 of baseline versus X4–X10 for many alternatives (we’ll quantify)."

Key differentiators to highlight in proofs:
- End-to-end framing: measure from client click -> first token + complete response; customers care about perceived wait, not just model latency.
- Workload realism: focus on multi-turn chat sessions with mixed short/long tails (avg 80–200 tokens/session, 5–12 turns).
- Cost amortization: include control-plane and ops assumptions for dedicated/self-hosted comparisons (e.g., reserved vs spot, SRE hours).
- Fallbacks & reliability: show graceful fallbacks (model variants, region routing) that preserve service.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Workloads: chat (multi-turn), summarization batch (100–500docs), embeddings flow (high-cardinality similarity).
- Scales: small pilot (10 RPS), mid (50 RPS), burst (200 RPS for 60s).
- Baselines: (A) Redwood hosted default config, (B) Redwood optimized (batching + cache + quantized model), (C) Leading MLP managed endpoint (anonymized), (D) self-host naive (single p4-like GPU), (E) self-host ops-aware (multi-node + caching).
- Metrics to capture: client-to-first-token ms (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec throughput, cost-per-1000-requests (incl infra + ops), error/retry rate, tail-latency under burst.

Measurement notes / methodology (must be consistent across comparisons):
- Use identical synthetic traffic profiles (recorded-real sessions where possible).
- Warm KV-caches and session caches before measurement window. Record warm vs cold windows separately.
- Include network RTT simulations for target regions (e.g., 20ms NA, 60ms EU, 120ms APAC) to reflect user-perceived latency.
- Normalize cost to USD/month per 10k MAU equivalent (we provide a conversion table).

Representative quick result we want to aim for in the first lab run (hypothesis):
- Redwood optimized vs managed baseline: p95 end-to-end latency 400ms vs 850ms (≈53% improvement); cost-per-active-user $0.18 vs $0.28 (≈36% savings) at 50 RPS mixed chat workload.

Competitive notes (high-level, non-attributed for field use):
- Large managed API providers: excellent model quality, simple UX, but conservative batching and limited prefix-cache; they favor lower-throughput single-tenant endpoints which increases unit cost for many mid-sized apps.
- Self-hosted runtimes (open-source + infra): can be cheaper at massive scale but require significant SRE investment; tail latency and KV/session-state handling are common stumbling blocks.
- Vertical inference vendors: focus on one optimization (quantization or kernel-level speedups) but often lack orchestration (fallbacks, per-route SLOs) so real-world cost/latency wins are less consistent.

Field scripts / SE talking points (short form):
- Hook: "Most customers we talk to measure latency from the user’s click, not from the model's first op. We optimize the full path — caching, routing, batching — so your users feel the difference at scale."
- Demo checklist: 1) Start with cold run to show cold vs warm impact. 2) Run a short burst to highlight tail-latency and fallback behavior. 3) Show cost-estimate overlay (Redwood dashboard) and a cost-amortization note that includes ops. 4) Run a second warm run showing steady-state p95/p99 improvements.
- Sample AE script (30s): "When we ran a 50 RPS mixed-chat profile, customers saw half the 95th percentile latency once we turned on session-aware caching and workload-aware batching — and the cost per active-user dropped by a third once autoscaling and spot capacity were factored in."

Evidence artifacts to attach for an initial field kit:
- Short 2–3 minute recording of a side-by-side warm-run (Redwood optimized vs managed baseline).
- CSV export of p50/p95/p99 across runs + cost calculations (s3 link above).
- Small slide: "How we measure" with diagram (client -> edge -> routing -> runtime -> model).
- Scripted lab runbook (commands + configs) for SEs to reproduce in <45 minutes.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Q: How much to disclose about the exact competitor config? Keep anonymized but ensure the comparison is fair and reproducible. Action: finalize competitor test templates with Legal. (JIRA-5472)
- Q: Ops amortization assumptions need standardization (hours per 1k MAU, cost/hour for SRE). Action: ask FinOps for a reasonable baseline.
- Need to finalize the stalled PR that adds our test harness to the perf repo (PR#114). Diego on it.

Risk & guardrails for public claims:
- Avoid absolute percentages without confidence intervals — use ranges (e.g., 30–60%) and note workload context.
- Don’t claim feature parity on model quality; only claim latency/cost improvements for specified workloads.
- For enterprise contracts, include a short appendix with raw CSVs and reproducible configs to satisfy procurement.

Next steps (near term):
1) SE dry run (Linnea) this week using recorded real sessions from two pilot customers.
2) Produce the short demo video and CSV artifacts.
3) Draft a one-pager for AE playbook that includes the 3 core claims and sample scripts (deliverable date: 2025-06-27).

Notes to self / brainstorming fragments (informal):
- Consider a "user-latency ladder" metric: measure from user-gesture -> actionable UI update (not necessarily final token). Could be a stronger hook for interactive apps.
- Could package an "ops-adjusted" cost calculator in the Redwood dashboard that auto-populates assumptions for Dedicated vs Private mode. Big win for sales enablement.
- Quick idea: short checklist for procurement: "Does your vendor expose per-route p95/p99? Do they provide cost amortization templates? Can they reproduce your workload?"

End of draft.

-- Asha
